questions.prompt: Complete the mixed conditional: "If I had taken that scholarship, I ___ in Paris right now."

options.text: would be
would have been
had been
was

questions.explanation: This is Mixed Conditional A: past condition (if + past perfect) → present result (would + base verb). 'Would be' correctly expresses the present consequence of a past unchosen action. "would have been" 'would have been' is the pure third conditional result — it implies a past consequence, but 'right now' signals a present one. "had been" is past perfect — wrong in the result clause. "was" is past simple — no modal, no conditional meaning.

questions.prompt: Identify the Mixed Conditional B sentence (present condition → past result).

options.text: If she had known, she would have told us.
If he weren't so stubborn, he would have agreed yesterday.
If you study hard, you'll pass.
If she had a car, she would drive to work.

questions.explanation: Mixed B has a present condition (if + past simple: 'weren't so stubborn' — he IS stubborn now) and a past result (would + have + pp: 'would have agreed yesterday'). "told us" is a pure third conditional (past → past). "If you study hard, you'll pass" is a first conditional (real future). "drive to work" is a second conditional (present hypothetical).

questions.prompt: Complete: "I wish I ___ to the dentist last month — the pain is terrible now."

options.text: went
would go
had gone
have gone

questions.explanation: The reference to 'last month' marks this as a past regret: 'wish + past perfect' is required — 'I wish I had gone'. "went" uses past simple — this pattern ('I wish I went') expresses a present wish, not a past regret. "would go" uses 'would go' — 'would' with the same subject as 'wish' for a state/action is wrong. "have gone" uses present perfect — not a valid 'wish' pattern.

questions.prompt: Read: "Sara is brilliant but very disorganised. She didn't submit her project on time and failed the module." Which sentence BEST describes the situation?

options.text: If she were more organised, she would pass the module.
If she had been more organised, she would pass the module now.
If she had been more organised, she would have passed the module.
Unless she is organised, she will fail.

questions.explanation: The text describes a past event (she failed) caused by a past condition (she wasn't organised then). A pure third conditional captures this: 'If she had been more organised, she would have passed.' "were" is a second conditional — implies she's not organised now and would pass in the future, missing the past event. "now" is a mixed conditional A — implies she's not organised now with a present result, but the text says she already failed. "will fail" is a first conditional about the future, which doesn't reflect the past situation.

options.text: If only I had checked my email sooner!
Unless he studies, he won't pass.
I wish he would arrive on time for once.
If I would have studied more, I would have passed.

questions.explanation: 'Would' must never go inside the if-clause of any conditional: 'If I would have studied' is wrong. The correct form is 'If I had studied more, I would have passed' (third conditional). "If only I had checked my email sooner!" correctly uses past perfect with 'if only' for a past regret. "Unless he studies, he won't pass" correctly uses 'unless'. "I wish he would arrive on time for once" correctly uses 'would' with 'wish' to express annoyance at someone else's behaviour.

questions.prompt: Complete both gaps: "___ you promise to be careful, you can borrow my camera; ___ you damage it, you'll have to replace it."

options.text: Provided that / unless
Unless / provided that
If only / unless
Provided that / if only

questions.explanation: 'Provided that you promise' sets a strict positive condition for borrowing. 'Unless you damage it' = 'If you don't damage it, you won't need to replace it' — a negative condition. "Unless / provided that" reverses them: 'Unless you promise' would mean 'if you don't promise', making the sentence block borrowing unless refused, which contradicts the offer. "If only / unless" uses 'if only' — this expresses a wish, not a condition. "Provided that / if only" uses 'if only' in the second clause — wrong register and meaning.
